text: Chapter 6 gave you functions like validate_row that decide whether a record is clean enough to load. Running the whole pipeline just to check if one function still works is slow and indirect — a unit test calls that function directly, with known input, and checks the exact output, in a fraction of a second.

pytest finds your tests automatically — any file named test underscore something, and any function inside it named test underscore something. No registration, no decorator. Assert is the whole mechanism: if the expression is True, the test passes; if not, pytest tells you exactly which assertion failed.

Don't stop at the happy path. Here we're also checking that a missing order_id and a zero amount both get rejected. A function that's only ever tested with good input can hide a bug in exactly the path your pipeline depends on to catch bad data — testing the rejection cases is what actually proves the function works.

Some functions are supposed to raise an exception on bad input — parse_amount should blow up on None rather than silently returning garbage. pytest.raises wraps the call and the test fails if that ValueError doesn't actually happen, confirming the guard clause is real and not just assumed.

Run it with pytest and the -v flag, and you get one line per test instead of just a dot per pass — handy while you're actively writing new tests and want to see exactly which one just ran, and that all five here come back PASSED.

Next: robust error handling. You'll move past the bare except clause and learn to catch specific exceptions, retry a flaky network call with backoff, and make a pipeline fail loudly instead of quietly limping along on bad data.
